concept.name: FX triangular arbitrage
concept.definition: The practice of exploiting a pricing discrepancy among three currencies by executing three trades — exchanging an initial currency for a second, the second for a third, and the third back into the initial — when the quoted cross exchange rate diverges from the implicit cross rate derived from the other two pairs. High-frequency studies find such opportunities are rare, small (often ~1 basis point) and fleeting (mostly lasting seconds or less).
concept.intuition: If EUR/USD and USD/JPY imply one EUR/JPY rate but a bank quotes another, you can cycle through the three pairs and end up with more than you started.
concept.mechanics: The arbitrageur computes the implicit cross rate S(a/b) = S(a/$) x S($/b) from quoted rates and compares it with the market cross quote, accounting for bid and ask on each leg. A profitable cycle exists only if the discrepancy exceeds transaction costs; electronic trading systems detect and exhaust such gaps in milliseconds, which is why opportunity incidence fell as algorithmic trading spread.
concept.formula: Implicit cross rate S(a/b) = S(a/$) x S($/b); a no-arbitrage condition requires the quoted cross to equal the implicit cross (within bid-ask bounds).
concept.failure_modes: Execution risk dominates: even millisecond delays between identifying the gap and filling all three legs mean one leg can re-price, leaving the arbitrageur with an unwanted position and a close-out cost equal to the price move that killed the gap. Fees, latency and competition from faster systems erode the thin margins.
concept.misconceptions: Triangular arbitrage is not an easy retail strategy: executable opportunities at sizes above a basis point or two are essentially competed away by professional low-latency systems before slower participants can act.
concept.example: If dealers quote EUR/USD 0.8171 (euros per dollar) and GBP/USD 1.4650, the implicit EUR/GBP is 1.1971; a bank offering pounds at EUR 1.1910 lets an arbitrageur cycle $5m through the three pairs for about $25,400 profit before costs.
